title: Chop wood, carry water
hookLine: Layman Pang's verse: the marvelous is in carrying water and chopping wood (Chan tradition)
carry: fully present to the weight of the bucket

cards: What would count as a miracle in your house? A bill that pays itself? A teenager who empties the dishwasher unasked?
In the Chan tradition, a man known as Layman Pang was asked by his teacher what his days had been like, and his answer, as it's handed down, is a short verse.
Its punch line, in paraphrase: my supernatural power, my marvelous activity, is carrying water and hauling firewood. No flying. No reading minds.
A bucket and a bundle of sticks. Today's word comes from that verse, in the shape people now pass around: chop wood.

teach.b: First, who's speaking. Layman means he wasn't a monk. Chan tradition remembers Pang as a householder with a family, who studied with Chan teachers and is remembered for sharp, plain answers.
So the verse comes from an ordinary life, not from behind monastery walls. Second, the turn in the verse.
It opens by saying his daily affairs are nothing special, then reaches for very big words, supernatural powers, marvelous functioning, and attaches them to the dullest jobs in the house.
The joke is serious: whatever is wonderful about awakening shows up in the bucket and the firewood, not somewhere else.
Third, the saying it turned into.
You may have heard: before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water; after enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. It shares Layman Pang's spirit, but the words aren't his.
His verse, as it's handed down, speaks of hauling firewood, not chopping it. Fourth, what changes if nothing changes. The chores stay the same; the water still has to be carried.
What the verse points to is the one carrying it.
A person can haul water while thinking of a hundred other places. Or a person can haul water. In Chan, that second way, fully present to the weight of the bucket, is not a step toward the practice.

how: In Chan and Zen practice, daily chores such as cooking, cleaning and carrying are treated as part of meditation, and Layman Pang's verse is often quoted to make the point.

o: a Zen exercise for building strength and focus
a monastery punishment of hard labor for mistakes
a saying that finds the marvelous in plain chores

games.q: you're Layman Pang. your teacher asks what your days have been like. where do you say the marvelous is?
games.why: his verse names carrying water and hauling firewood as his supernatural power and marvelous activity.

practice: Sitting is a chore too: feel the weight of the body in the seat, the way a bucket pulls on the arm, and the breath carried in and carried out.

When the mind leaves for a hundred other places, notice where it went and pick the bucket back up. Let it be nothing special, and see whether that's the same as dull; if you pray, you can offer it in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Chop wood. From Layman Pang's Chan verse: the marvelous is found in carrying water and firewood, in the plain work of a day. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, from Layman Pang's verse: hauling firewood. the verse pairs it with carrying water.

carryVoice: Your line: fully present to the weight of the bucket. Nothing special, and that's the marvel. Day nine hundred.
